Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Sofia Ramos (Aurora Finance - Head of ML), Ben Thompson (Aurora - Platform), Priya Singh (Aurora - CTO)

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone thanks for making time today, really excited to walk through Redwood Optimize recommendations \u0014 particularly batching and the prefix slash KV cache \u0014 to see how we can drop your token spend and keep p95 latency under your SLO.
[00:12] Sofia: Thanks Maya, appreciate it. Quick context: our traffic is mostly short queries for customer support summarization and routing, so many requests are ~120-250 tokens. We have occasional long analytics requests but they are low QPS. Our big pain is cost \u0014 monthly token bill spiked last quarter \u0014 and we need to keep sub-400ms p95 for the realtime routing.
[00:35] Liam: Great context, Sofia. For those workloads, Optimize typically focuses on two knobs: batching to improve GPU throughput, and prefix or KV cache to avoid regenerating common prefixes like greetings, context, or system prompts. We'll show the cost model math and a recommended pilot config.
[00:50] Ben: Quick Q on infra: we're currently on hosted endpoints but are evaluating Redwood Dedicated for predictable throughput. Any difference in Optimize recommendations between hosted and dedicated?
[01:05] Liam: The core recommendations are the same; Dedicated gives you more headroom to set larger batch sizes and longer kv cache lifetimes because you control the capacity. In hosted, we may recommend slightly tighter batch sizing to meet your p95 SLOs and use dynamic routing to fall back to smaller-capacity instances if needed.
[01:25] Priya: Also, do we need to change our whole request pattern? Our app calls the API per message, not as a streaming chat.
[01:33] Maya: Not necessarily. We can often achieve batching at the gateway or with Redwood SDK batching features without changing your app. There are two approaches: client-side micro-batching (aggregate several requests before send) or server-side continuous batching which Redwood supports. For real-time routing with 300-400ms p95 needs, server-side shorter batch windows (10-30ms) usually work best.
[02:02] Sofia: Can you show the cost model? I want an estimate for our monthly 1B token usage baseline and expected savings.
[02:09] Liam: Sure; here's a simplified run-through \u0014 sorry if auto-transcript makes numbers weird. Baseline hosted model cost for your current model (open Llama variant) is X per 1M tokens; with batching and prefix/KV we typically see 25-45% token-equivalent cost reduction depending on cache hit rate. For Aurora, with your 1B tokens and an observed 30% common prefix overlap, you could see roughly 30% less generation tokens, plus batching reduces per-token GPU time lowering effective unit cost.
[02:44] Ben: That sounds promising. When you say prefix/KV cache, do you mean storing the KV cache for prefixes (like system priming) so downstream requests don't re-run those tokens? How does that affect memory and state?
[02:58] Liam: Exactly. Prefix or KV cache stores the key-value attention caches for tokens you reuse frequently \u0014 think system prompts, user profile snippets. Instead of re-encoding those tokens every request we append the cached KV state and only compute the new tokens. Memory impact is per cached prefix per model and per GPU shard; Optimize gives a recommendation for which prefixes to store and time-to-live (TTL). For instance, storing 50 prefixes per customer with 2-3 MB per prefix is usually reasonable.
[03:28] Sofia: Are there cases where cache hurts latency?
[03:33] Liam: If your prefix cache TTL is long and you cache very large contexts, retrieval and state merging can add a small constant overhead, but it's almost always less than the compute saved. The bigger risk is combinatorial explosion of prefixes \u0014 we recommend canonicalizing prefixes (normalize templates) to keep hit rates high.
[03:51] Maya: I'll pause and show a quick slide I sent earlier (link: deck.redwood/optimize/pilot). (brief screen share noise)
[04:03] Maya: Slide shows typical tradeoffs: small batches minimize p95 latency but get less throughput; larger batches improve token/sec and lower cost per token but increase tail latency. With KV caching you get both lower compute and sometimes lower latency because fewer tokens are recomputed.
[04:24] Ben: For our routing latency requirement, what's the sweet spot?
[04:29] Liam: For 300-400ms p95 and 120-250 token requests, we usually keep batch windows around 10-30ms and target effective batch sizes of 4-12 requests depending on concurrency. That gives most of the batching benefit without moving p95 above your threshold. In Dedicated you'd be able to push batch size higher for cost gains.
[04:52] Sofia: How do you measure hit rate? We have many different user prompts that are templated but sometimes micro-personalized.
[05:00] Liam: Two ways: offline analysis of past traffic to canonicalize and compute theoretical hit rate, and live evaluation during pilot by enabling prefix metrics in the console. We show per-prefix hit rate, bytes saved, and token reduction. For templated prompts, micro-personalization usually doesn't kill hit rates if you normalize variable fields (IDs, timestamps) and factor them out of prefix templates.
[05:24] Priya: Security question \u0014 if we cache prefix state, does that store any PII on Redwood? How's that encrypted and audited?
[05:33] Maya: Great question. Cached prefixes are encrypted at rest; for Dedicated and Private deployments you control the KMS/HSM. We also provide audit logs for cache reads/writes in the Console's observability tab. We'll share SOC2/ISO docs and specifics in the security packet.
[05:51] Ben: Can we see an example of the Optimize cost table?
[05:54] Liam: Yeah I'll read out an example from the deck \u0014 apologies for numbers if transcript warps them. Baseline cost: $X per 1M tokens (current model). With batching improvements we estimate 10-18% lower GPU time per token, and with prefix/KV cache at 30% hit rate additional 25% effective token reduction. Combined you get net 32-40% cost reduction in many customer cases. For Aurora we modeled a conservative 28% savings to set expectations.
[06:27] Sofia: Do you have real customer case studies?
[06:31] Maya: Yes \u0014 NovaBank and Starlite Finance (we shared benchmarks). They saw 25-35% token-equivalent reductions and improved p95 for short-message workloads via small batch windows plus prefix caching. I'll attach the PDFs after the call.
[06:46] Ben: For the pilot, what telemetry do you need from our side to validate results?
[06:52] Liam: Sample traffic logs (anonymized), token-level traces, and your latency SLOs. We prefer request-level histograms and a small sample of full requests. We'll provide a benchmark harness (k6 + token trace replay) that you can run in your environment or against Redwood staging.
[07:10] Priya: On the contract side, if the pilot shows good results, what's the usual next step \u0014 Dedicated reservation?
[07:16] Maya: Often teams move to a reserved Dedicated capacity or higher committed tiers on hosted, depending on security needs. We'll include a cost comparison in the pilot deliverable showing Dedicated vs Hosted at scale with expected unit economics.
[07:30] Sofia: I want to dig into a technical corner \u0014 we have long tails where some requests are 1k tokens. How does caching interact with long contexts?
[07:39] Liam: For long tails, the insight is to cache the stable prefix (system + user profile + recent context) and only run the long tail tokens fresh. If the long tail is rare, caching reduces a high fraction of average compute. For extreme long sequences, we also recommend quantized model variants or sequence-sliced execution.
[07:58] Ben: Any risk of model incompressibility where caching semantics change model outputs?
[08:04] Liam: There is a slight risk if your prompts rely on dynamic tokens inserted into the prefix (e.g., changing system priming). We recommend canonicalization and tests in the eval harness to detect regressions. Redwood Optimize ties quality regressions to prompt sets and will flag divergence beyond a threshold.
[08:25] Sofia: What's the overhead for adding prefix canonicalization to our pipeline?
[08:29] Maya: Minimal \u0014 typically a small normalization step to strip IDs, timestamps, and reorder nonsignificant fields. We can provide a reference library snippet for Node/Python to do this.
[08:40] Liam: I'm going to open the Console demo briefly to show the KV metrics and the cost model matrix. (noise) On the Console you can toggle time windows for batching, see projected cost per 1M tokens for each config, and simulate hit rates.
[09:05] Maya: (pointing) Here is the pilot recommendation: 2-week pilot, run on a small dedicated pool of 1-2 GPU instances in Redwood staging, enable prefix cache for top 50 templates with TTL 24h, batch window 25ms, target effective batch size 6. We'll run daily checkpoints and share a final dashboard.
[09:28] Priya: That seems reasonable. Question on data retention for cached prefixes \u0014 TTL 24h is fine but can we set shorter retention for personal PII?
[09:38] Maya: Yes you can set per-prefix policies; Optimize supports marking prefixes as sensitive and setting zero retention or encrypt-only flags. We'll include a config example.
[09:50] Ben: How intrusive is the SDK integration? Our gateway is Go-based.
[09:55] Liam: We have a Go SDK and HTTP proxy pattern that requires minimal changes. If you want to keep one net-new service, you can run a small batching proxy that aggregates requests. We'll share the proxy example.
[10:07] Sofia: Ok let's recap next steps \u0014 Maya, you'll send pricing and the pilot doc?
[10:12] Maya: Yes: pilot pricing sheet, runbook, security packet. Liam will attach the benchmark harness and a sample config.
[10:19] Priya: We'll send sample traffic and confirm kickoff date.
[10:22] Maya: Great. Any other open concerns?
[10:25] Ben: One small one \u0014 are there known gotchas with k8s autoscaling and batching collisions?
[10:31] Liam: Autoscaling can cause transient drops in batch sizes; Optimize suggests warm pools and a small buffer to keep batch efficiency. In Dedicated you have more control. We'll include a recommended autoscaler config for k8s.
[10:45] Sofia: Sounds good. Thanks, everyone.
[10:48] Maya: Thanks all \u0014 we'll follow up by EOD Friday with the packet and let's tentatively set pilot start for next Tuesday.

(End of recording)
